title: Pity and hatred cannot go together
source_text: Οὐκ οἶδα δ᾿ ὅπως τὰ ἄμικτα καὶ οὐ πεφυκότα ἅμα συμβαίνειν ἀνθρωπίνῃ φύσει συναγαγὼν εἶπε τὸ βιβλίον ἐκεῖνο ἐλέους καὶ μίσους ἄξιον εἶναι. πᾶς γὰρ ὁμολογήσει τὸν ἐλεούμενον μὴ μισεῖσθαι, ὅτ᾿ ἐλεεῖται, καὶ τὸν μισούμενον μὴ ἐλεεῖσθαι, ὅτε μισεῖται. διὰ τοῦτο δὲ μὴ προκεῖσθαι ἐλέγχειν φησὶ ταῦτα ὁ Κέλσος, ἐπεὶ οἴεται αὐτὰ παντί που δῆλα εἶναι καὶ πρὸ τοῦ ἐπαγομένου λογικῶς ἐλέγχου ὡς φαῦλα καὶ ἐλέους καὶ μίσους ἄξια. παρακαλοῦμεν δὲ τὸν ἐντυγχάνοντα τῇ ἀπολογίᾳ ταύτῃ πρὸς τὴν Κέλσου κατηγορίαν γεγραμμένῃ ἀνασχέσθαι καὶ ἐπακοῦσαι τῶν συγγραμμάτων ἡμῶν καὶ ὅση δύναμις ἐκ τῶν γεγραμμένων στοχάσασθαι τῆς προαιρέσεως τῶν γραψάντων καὶ τῆς συνειδήσεως καὶ τῆς διαθέσεως· εὑρήσει γὰρ ἄνδρας, διαπύρως περὶ ὧν ὑπειλήφασι διατεινομένους, τινὰς δὲ ἐμφαίνοντας καὶ τὸ ἱστορίαν ἑωραμένην καὶ καταληφθεῖσαν ἀναγράφειν ὡς παράδοξον καὶ γραφῆς ἀξίαν ἐπὶ ὠφελείᾳ τῶν ἀκουσομένων. ἢ τολμάτω τις λέγειν μὴ πάσης ὠφελείας εἶναι πηγὴν καὶ ἀρχὴν τὸ πιστεῦσαι τῷ τῶν ὅλων θεῷ καὶ πάντα πράττειν κατ᾿ ἀναφορὰν τοῦ ἐκείνῳ ἀρέσκειν περὶ οὑτινοσοῦν καὶ μηδὲν ἀπάρεστον αὐτῷ μηδ᾿ ἐνθυμεῖσθαι, ὡς οὐ μόνον λόγων καὶ ἔργων ἀλλὰ καὶ διαλογισμῶν κριθησομένων. καὶ τίς ἂν ἄλλος λόγος ἐπιστρεφέστερον προσάγοι τὴν ἀνθρωπίνην φύσιν τῷ εὖ ζῆν ὡς ἡ πίστις ἢ ἡ διάληψις περὶ τοῦ πάντ᾿ ἐφορᾶν τὸν ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεὸν τὰ ὑφ᾿ ἡμῶν λεγόμενα καὶ πραττόμενα ἀλλὰ καὶ λογιζόμενα; παραβαλέτω γὰρ ὁ βουλόμενος ἄλλην ὁδὸν, ἐπιστρέφουσαν ἅμα καὶ βελτιοῦσαν οὐ μόνον ἕνα που καὶ δεύτερον ἀλλ᾿ ὅση δύναμις καὶ πλείστους ὅσους, ἵνα τις τῇ παραθέσει ἀμφοτέρων τῶν ὁδῶν ἀκριβῶς κατανοήσῃ τὸν διατιθέντα πρὸς τὸ καλὸν λόγον.
pass_a_gloss: I do not know how, having brought together (συνάγω) things unmixable (ἄμικτος) and not naturally (φύω) occurring together in human nature, he said that book is worthy of pity and hatred. For everyone will agree that the one pitied (ἐλεέω) is not hated when he is pitied, and the one hated is not pitied when he is hated. For this reason Celsus says it is not proposed to refute these, since he thinks them plain to everyone even before the logically applied (ἐπάγω, λογικῶς) refutation, as worthless (φαῦλος) and worthy of pity and hatred. We exhort (παρακαλέω) the one reading (ἐντυγχάνω) this defence (ἀπολογία) written against Celsus's accusation (κατηγορία) to bear and listen to our writings and, as far as possible, from what is written to conjecture (στοχάζομαι) the purpose (προαίρεσις) of the writers, and the conscience (συνείδησις) and the disposition (διάθεσις); for he will find men ardently (διαπύρως) contending (διατείνομαι) for what they have accepted (ὑπολαμβάνω), and some showing (ἐμφαίνω) that they record (ἀναγράφω) a story (ἱστορία) seen and grasped (καταλαμβάνω) as marvellous (παράδοξος) and worthy of writing for the benefit (ὠφέλεια) of the future hearers. Or let someone dare (τολμάω) to say that it is not the source (πηγή) and beginning (ἀρχή) of all benefit to believe the God of all and to do all with reference (ἀναφορά) to pleasing (ἀρέσκω) him about anything whatever and not even to ponder (ἐνθυμέομαι) anything displeasing (ἀπάρεστος) to him, as not only words and deeds but even reasonings (διαλογισμός) will be judged (κρίνω). And what other teaching (λόγος) would bring human nature more turningly (ἐπιστρεφέστερον, more powerfully) to living well than faith or the conception (διάληψις) that the God over all oversees (ἐφοράω) the things said and done but also reckoned (λογίζομαι) by us? Let him who wishes compare (παραβάλλω) another way (ὁδός), converting (ἐπιστρέφω) at once and improving (βελτιόω) not only one and a second but as far as possible as many as possible, so that by the comparison (παράθεσις) of both ways one may accurately understand (κατανοέω) the teaching that disposes (διατίθημι) to the good.
pass_b_english: I do not know how Celsus could bring together things that do not mix and that by nature cannot occur at the same time in human nature, and say that the book deserves pity and hatred. For everyone will agree that someone who is pitied is not hated while he is pitied, and someone who is hated is not pitied while he is hated. Celsus says that it is not his purpose to refute these things, because he thinks they are plain to everyone even before any reasoned refutation is brought against them, as worthless and deserving of pity and hatred. But we urge the reader of this defence, written against Celsus’s accusation, to bear with our writings and listen to them, and, as far as he can, to infer from what is written the purpose of those who wrote it, their conscience, and their disposition. For he will find men who contend ardently for what they have come to believe, and some who make it clear that they are recording a story they had seen and understood, as something marvellous and worth writing down for the benefit of those who were to hear it.

Or let someone dare to say that it is not the source and beginning of every benefit to believe in the God of the universe, to do everything with a view to pleasing him in every matter whatever, and not even to think of anything that displeases him, since not only our words and deeds but even our thoughts will be judged. And what other teaching could more forcefully lead human nature to live well than faith, or the conviction, that the God over all watches over everything we say and do, and even what we think? Let anyone who wishes compare with it another way that both converts and improves, not just one or two people, but as many as possible, so that by comparing the two ways one may understand exactly which teaching disposes people toward the good.

choices.choice: ἀνασχέσθαι καὶ ἐπακοῦσαι: 'bear with our writings and listen to them' (was 'be patient and listen')
perfect ἑωραμένην: 'a story they had seen'; ἀκουσομένων 'those who were to hear it'
ὅση δύναμις καὶ πλείστους ὅσους: 'as many as possible' (was 'as far as possible a very great many')
no Scripture quotation in this chapter; possible echoes left uncited, noted

'The book' is the Disputation of Jason and Papiscus (4.52). 'A story they had seen and understood' (ἱστορίαν ἑωραμένην καὶ καταληφθεῖσαν) points to the eyewitness Gospel writers; no single verse is quoted. The judgement of words, deeds and thoughts may echo Matthew 12:36 or Romans 2:16, and God seeing all may echo Hebrews 4:13, but none is clear enough to cite inline. λόγος rendered 'teaching' in the last two sentences. ἐπιστρεφέστερον ('more forcefully', literally 'in a more turning way') plays on ἐπιστρέφουσαν ('converts') in the next sentence. διὰ τοῦτο ... ἐπεί is carried by 'because' alone. ὅση δύναμις καὶ πλείστους ὅσους rendered 'as many as possible'.
